Estimating Circumference

Infinite SeriesAlgorithmsCounting
Game: Watch straight-sided shapes close in on the curved edge of a circle.
How to play: Move the slider to add sides to the polygon and watch the perimeter readings tighten around the circumference.

Look for the math

A polygon with straight sides can never be a circle — but with enough sides its perimeter gets as close as you like.

Inscribed and circumscribed

A regular n-gon inside a circle of radius R has perimeter P = 2nR·sin(π/n); one outside has C = 2nR·tan(π/n). The circle's circumference 2πR is squeezed between them. As n grows, the inscribed perimeter increases, the circumscribed one decreases, and the gap between them shrinks to zero — the idea Archimedes used more than two thousand years ago with n = 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96.

What the check found

The logic test checks all n from 3 to 96: the squeeze holds, the two sequences really are monotone, the gap shrinks, and summing the chord lengths independently matches the sine formula. At 96 sides the inscribed perimeter is within 0.01 of 2π for a unit circle.

Slide to 96 sides. How much bigger is the circumscribed perimeter than the inscribed one?
